definition: To speak about someone or something as if it has little worth or importance.
example: Rather than disparage her rival's design, the architect pointed out its strengths.
nuance: To criticize can be fair and constructive, but to disparage is to talk something down and make it seem worth less than it is.
prompt: A chef learns that a new restaurant has opened across the street.
options: The jealous chef began to disparage the new menu, calling it bland and unoriginal.
Hoping to disparage the crowd outside, the chef waved everyone toward the bus stop.
The chef chose to disparage the newcomer by calling its pastries the finest in town.
The two kitchens serve such disparage dishes that they rarely compete for diners.
reasons: Scornful remarks meant to lower the rival's standing fit the word exactly.
Scattering a group of people is dispersing, not speaking scornfully of something.
High praise lifts a reputation instead of running it down.
This needs the look-alike adjective disparate; the verb cannot mean very different.

practice.prompt: Students discuss a classmate's entry at the science fair.
options: After losing the prize, the student began to disparage of ever winning again.
The judges had to disparage each project by measuring its height with a ruler.
Some classmates tried to disparage the model as babyish, but the judges admired it.
To disparage the volcano model, one classmate described it as clever and carefully built.
reasons: Losing hope is despair; the phrase mixes up a look-alike word.
Taking neutral measurements involves no scorn or belittling remarks.
Calling the project childish is a dismissive attempt to make it seem worthless.
Admiring words raise the project's standing rather than lowering it.
